title: An Agent-Based Approach to Modeling Bacterial Multicellularity
text:
Abstract
This dissertation presents an Agent-Based Model (ABM) framework for studying bacterial multicellularity and the emergence of complex spatial patterns from local cellular interactions…
Keywords: Agent-based modeling, bacterial multicellularity, quorum sensing, biofilms

title: Part I: Applications
text:
This part applies the modeling framework developed in Part I to specific bacterial systems. Each chapter examines a distinct biological case study, demonstrating how agent-based models can capture emergent multicellular behavior from local cellular interactions.
Chapters in this part:

Chapter 10 explores Streptomyces developmental biology and aerial hyphae formation
Chapter 11 investigates Bacillus subtilis biofilm architecture and differentiation
Chapter 12 analyzes synthetic gene regulatory networks and programmable behavior
Chapter 13 examines extracellular matrix polymers and mechanical interactions

title: 1  Analytical solution of the 2D diffusion equation with Neumann boundary conditions
text:
2 Solving \(T(t)\)
Let’s first find the analytical solution to the following diffusion equation:
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = D \nabla^2 u
\tag{1.1}\]
The equation is defined on an two dimensional domain \(\Omega = [0,L_x] \times [0,L_y]\) with reflective boundary conditions. The initial condition is given by a set of \(N\) point-like sources located at positions \(\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^N\) with strengths \(\{A_i\}_{i=1}^N\): \[
u(x,y,0) = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i \delta(x-x_i) \delta(y-y_i)
\tag{1.2}\]
For some purposes, such as plotting purposes, we could approximate the Dirac’s delta functions using narrow Gaussian functions. If aproximated by narrow Gaussian functions, the initial condition becomes:
\[
u(x,y,0) = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i \frac{1}{2 \pi \sigma^2} \exp\left(-\frac{(x-x_i)^2 + (y-y_i)^2}{2 \sigma^2}\right)
\tag{1.3}\] For example, if there were 7 point-like sources randomly located in the domain with strengths \(A_i = i\), \(\sigma = 0.02\), in a domain of size \(L_x = L_y = 1\), the plot of the initial condition would look like this:
The Neumann boundary conditions are given by: \[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=0} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=L_x} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\Big|_{y=0} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\Big|_{y=L_y} = 0
\tag{1.4}\]
For implementing the method of separation of variables, we will assume that the solution can be written as a product:
\[
u(x,y,t) = X(x) Y(y) T(t)
\tag{1.5}\]
Substituting equation Equation 1.5 into equation Equation 1.1, we have:
\[
X Y \frac{dT}{dt} = D \left( Y T \frac{d^2X}{dx^2} + X T \frac{d^2Y}{dy^2} \right)
\]
and dividing both sides by \(D X Y T\) gives: \[
\frac{1}{DT} \frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{1}{X} \frac{d^2X}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{Y} \frac{d^2Y}{dy^2}
\tag{1.6}\] The left side of equation Equation 1.6 depends only on time \(t\), while the right side depends only on the spatial variables \(x\) and \(y\). So, the left-hand side and the right-hand side are completely independent of each other. The only way for two independent functions to be equal to each other for all values of \(x\), \(y\), and \(t\) is if they are both equal to the same constant. Therefore, we will denote this constant as \(-\lambda\). So, the left-hand side is equal to:
\[
\frac{1}{DT} \frac{dT}{dt} = -\lambda
\]
and the right-hand side is equal to:
\[
\frac{1}{X} \frac{d^2X}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{Y} \frac{d^2Y}{dy^2} = -\lambda
\]
This leads to three ordinary differential equations: \[
\frac{dT}{dt} + D \lambda T = 0
\tag{1.7}\] \[
\frac{d^2X}{dx^2} + \lambda_x X = 0
\tag{1.8}\] \[
\frac{d^2Y}{dy^2} + \lambda_y  Y = 0
\tag{1.9}\] where \(\lambda = \lambda_x + \lambda_y\).
Now we can solve each of these equations separately.
The solution to equation Equation 1.7 is:
\[
T(t) = C_t e^{-D \lambda t}
\tag{2.1}\]
This is a decaying exponential function, which decaying rate is determined by the constant \(\lambda\). For a constant \(C_t = 1\), the plot of \(T(t)\) for different values of \(\lambda\) is shown below:
Code
viewof lambda = Inputs.range([-0.5, 0.5], {step: 0.1, value: 1, label: "lambda"})
ts = Array.from({length: 800}, (_, i) => i/199 * 5)
Ts = ts.map(t => Math.exp(-lambda * t))
solutionTimePlot = {
  const div = document.createElement("div");
  div.style.height = "500px";
  div.style.width = "100%";

  Plotly.newPlot(div, [{
    x: ts, 
    y: Ts,
    mode: "lines",
  }], {    
    yaxis: {title: "T(t)"}, 
    xaxis: {title: "t"},
    width: 750,
    height: 500,
    

  });
  return div;
}
Here we can see that for positive values of \(\lambda\), the function decays to zero as time increases, whereas for negative values of \(\lambda\), the function grows rapidly with time. However, as we will see later, the boundary conditions will restrict the possible values of \(\lambda\) to be non-negative, ensuring that \(T(t)\) always decays over time.

title: 1  Analytical solution of the 2D diffusion equation with Neumann boundary conditions
text:
3.2 Zero-vaued \(\lambda_x\)

If \(\lambda_x = 0\), then \(\frac{d^2X}{dx^2} = 0\). Integrating this equation twice gives:

\[
X(x) = A + B x
\tag{3.5}\] Applying the boundary conditions: \[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} = B = 0
\] and \[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=L_x} = B = 0
\] Thus, the solution simplifies to: \[
X(x) = A
\]
crumbs: 1  Analytical solution of the 2D diffusion equation with Neumann boundary conditions

title: 1  Analytical solution of the 2D diffusion equation with Neumann boundary conditions
text:
3.3 Negative \(\lambda_x\)

If \(\lambda_x < 0\), then \(k = \pm \sqrt{ |\lambda_x|}\). This means that the 2 independent solutions are:

\[
X_1(x) = e^{\sqrt{ |\lambda_x|} x}
\] and \[
X_2(x) = e^{-\sqrt{ |\lambda_x|} x}
\] which leads to the general solution: \[
X(x) = C_1 e^{\sqrt{ |\lambda_x|} x} + C_2 e^{-\sqrt{ |\lambda_x|} x}
\]
\[
X(x) = A \cosh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} x) + B \sinh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} x)
\tag{3.6}\]
The derivative of Equation 3.6 is: \[
\frac{dX}{dx} = A \sqrt{|\lambda_x|} \sinh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} x) + B \sqrt{|\lambda_x|} \cosh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} x)
\]
Applying the first boundary condition:
\[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} = B \sqrt{|\lambda_x|} = 0 \implies B = 0
\]
Thus, the solution simplifies to:
\[
X(x) = A \cosh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} x)
\]
and applying the second boundary condition:
\[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=L_x} = A \sqrt{|\lambda_x|} \sinh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} L_x) = 0
\]
Since \(A \neq 0\) and \(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} \neq 0\), we have:
\[
\sinh(\sqrt{|\lambda_x|} L_x) = 0 \implies \sqrt{|\lambda_x|} L_x = 0 \implies \lambda_x = 0
\] This contradicts our initial assumption that \(\lambda_x < 0\). Therefore, there are no solutions for \(\lambda_x < 0\).

title: 1  Analytical solution of the 2D diffusion equation with Neumann boundary conditions
text:
4.1 Infinite sum of eigenmodes
Substituting these results back into the temporal equation Equation 1.7, we find that a separated solution of the form \[
u_{n,m}(x,y,t) = X_n(x) Y_m(y) T_{n,m}(t)
\] satisfies the diffusion equation Equation 1.1 with Neumann boundary conditions, where each separated solution (or eigenmode) associated with the pair \((n,m)\) can be written as \[
u_{n,m}(x,y,t)
= \Phi_{n,m}(x,y)\, e^{-D \lambda_{n,m} t}
= A_n B_m \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right)
               \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right)
               e^{-D \lambda_{n,m} t},
\] where the overall multiplicative factor \(A_n B_m\) can again be absorbed into a single mode amplitude.
Because the set \(\{\Phi_{n,m}\}_{n,m \ge 0}\) forms an orthogonal basis of \(L^2([0,L_x]\times[0,L_y])\) adapted to the Neumann boundary conditions, any sufficiently regular initial condition can be expanded uniquely as a series in these spatial eigenfunctions. By linearity and superposition, the general solution to the diffusion equation Equation 1.1 takes the form \[
u(x,y,t)
= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty}
  C_{n,m}\,
  \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right)
  \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right)
  e^{-D \lambda_{n,m} t},
\tag{4.2}\]
and the coefficients \(C_{n,m}\) are determined by projecting the initial condition Equation 1.2 onto the spatial eigenfunctions \(\Phi_{n,m}\).

title: 1  Analytical solution of the 2D diffusion equation with Neumann boundary conditions
text:
4.2 Determining the constants \(C_{n,m}\)
To find the constants \(C_{n,m}\), we can use the initial condition Equation 1.3. Evaluating the initial condition at \(t=0\) gives:
\[
u(x,y,0) =
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} C_{n,m} \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right)
\tag{4.3}\]
We just need to find a way to calculate the coefficients \(C_{n,m}\). To do this, we will use the orthogonality property of the cosines to transform the infinite series problem into a integral calculation.
crumbs: 1  Analytical solution of the 2D diffusion equation with Neumann boundary conditions

title: 1  Analytical solution of the 2D diffusion equation with Neumann boundary conditions
text:
4.3 Orthogonality
For any fixed \(L > 0\), the cosine functions \(\{\cos(\frac{n \pi x}{L})\}_{n=0}^{\infty}\) form an orthogonal basis on the interval \([0,L]\) with respect to the inner product. This means that if we have two different functions from this set, say \(\phi_n(x)\) and \(\phi_m(x)\): \[
\phi_{n}(x) = \cos\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L}\right) \quad n \in \mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}
\]
\[
\phi_{m}(x) = \cos\left(\frac{m \pi x}{L}\right) \quad m \in \mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}
\]
then the integral of their product is zero if \(n \neq m\). Mathematically, this orthogonality condition can be expressed as: \[
\int_0^L \phi_{n}(x) \phi_{m}(x) \, dx =
\begin{cases}
\frac{L}{2} & \text{if } n=m \text{ and } n,m > 0 \\
L & \text{if } n=m=0 \\
0 & \text{if } n \neq m
\end{cases}
\tag{4.4}\]

Figure 4.1: Plot of cosine functions to illustrate orthogonality




Let’s define a new set of eigenfunctions:
\[
\phi_{p,q}(x,y) = \cos\left(\frac{p \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{q \pi}{L_y} y\right) \quad p,q \in \mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}
\]
Now, we multiply both sides of equation Equation 4.3 by \(\phi_{p,q}(x,y)\) to get:
\[
u(x,y,0) \phi_{p,q}(x,y) =
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} C_{n,m} \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right) \cos\left(\frac{p \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{q \pi}{L_y} y\right)
\tag{4.5}\]
Next, we integrate both sides of equation Equation 4.5 over the domain \(\Omega\):
\[
\int_0^{L_x} \int_0^{L_y} u(x,y,0) \phi_{p,q}(x,y) \, dy \, dx =
\] \[
=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} C_{n,m} \int_0^{L_x} \int_0^{L_y} \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right)\cos\left(\frac{p \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{q \pi}{L_y} y\right) \, dy \, dx
\tag{4.6}\]
Rearranging the right-hand side of equation Equation 4.6 gives:
\[
=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} C_{n,m}\underbrace{ \left( \int_0^{L_x} \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{p \pi}{L_x} x\right) \, dx \right)}_{I_{x}(n,p)} \underbrace{\left( \int_0^{L_y} \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right) \cos\left(\frac{q \pi}{L_y} y\right) \, dy \right)}_{I_{y}(m,q)}
\tag{4.7}\]
Here is where the orthogonality property shown in equation Equation 4.4 comes into play. The integrals \(I_{x}(n,p)\) and \(I_{y}(m,q)\) will have the following values:
\[
I_{x}(n,p) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{L_x}{2} & \text{if } n=p \text{ and } n,p > 0 \\
L_x & \text{if } n=p=0 \\
0 & \text{if } n \neq p
\end{cases}
\] \[
I_{y}(m,q) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{L_y}{2} & \text{if } m=q \text{ and } m,q > 0 \\
L_y & \text{if } m=q=0 \\
0 & \text{if } m \neq q
\end{cases}
\]
This means that all the terms in the infinite sums in equation Equation 4.7 will be zero except for the single term where \(n=p\) and \(m=q\).
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} C_{n,m} I_{x}(n,p) I_{y}(m,q) = C_{p,q} I_{x}(p,p) I_{y}(q,q)
\tag{4.8}\]
Then, we can rewrite equation Equation 4.6 as:
\[
\int_0^{L_x} \int_0^{L_y} u(x,y,0) \phi_{p,q}(x,y) \, dy \, dx = C_{p,q} N_{x}(p) N_{y}(q)
\tag{4.9}\]
where
\[
N_{x}(p) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{L_x}{2} & \text{if } p > 0 \\
L_x & \text{if } p=0
\end{cases}
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
N_{y}(q) =
\begin{cases}
\frac{L_y}{2} & \text{if } q > 0 \\
L_y & \text{if } q=0
\end{cases}
\]
Finally, we can solve for the coefficients \(C_{p,q}\):
\[
C_{p,q} = \frac{1}{N_{x}(p) N_{y}(q)} \int_0^{L_x} \int_0^{L_y} u(x,y,0) \phi_{p,q}(x,y) \, dy \, dx
\tag{4.10}\]
But wait, we were looking for \(C_{n,m}\), not \(C_{p,q}\). However, since the only term that survived in the infinite sums was the one where \(n=p\) and \(m=q\), we can simply substitute \(p\) by \(n\) and \(q\) by \(m\), leading to the final expression for the coefficients \(C_{n,m}\):
\[
C_{n,m} = \frac{1}{N_{x}(n) N_{y}(m)} \int_0^{L_x} \int_0^{L_y} u(x,y,0) \phi_{n,m}(x,y) \, dy \, dx
\]
which is the same as:
\[
C_{n,m} = \frac{4 \varepsilon_{n} \varepsilon_{m}}{L_x L_y} \int_0^{L_x} \int_0^{L_y} u(x,y,0) \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right) \, dy \, dx
\tag{4.11}\]
where
\[
\varepsilon_{q} =
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{2} & \text{if } q=0 \\
1 & \text{if } q > 0
\end{cases}
\]

title: 1  Analytical solution of the 2D diffusion equation with Neumann boundary conditions
text:
4.4 Integrating with the initial condition
Now we can substitute the initial condition Equation 1.2 into equation Equation 4.11 to calculate the coefficients \(C_{n,m}\):
\[
C_{n,m} = \frac{4 \varepsilon_{n} \varepsilon_{m}}{L_x L_y} \int_0^{L_x} \int_0^{L_y} \left( \sum_{i=1}^N A_i \delta(x-x_i) \delta(y-y_i) \right) \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right) \, dy \, dx
\] Since the integral of the sum is equal to the sum of the integrals, we can rewrite this as:
\[C_{n,m} = \frac{4 \varepsilon_{n} \varepsilon_{m}}{L_x L_y} \sum_{i=1}^N A_i \int_0^{L_x} \int_0^{L_y} \delta(x-x_i) \delta(y-y_i) \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right) \, dy \, dx
\] Since the domain is rectangular and we can separate the integrals, we have:
\[
C_{n,m} = \frac{4 \varepsilon_{n} \varepsilon_{m}}{L_x L_y} \sum_{i=1}^N A_i \left( \int_0^{L_x} \delta(x-x_i) \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right) \, dx \right) \left( \int_0^{L_y} \delta(y-y_i) \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right) \, dy \right)
\]
Here we can use the sifting property of the Dirac delta function, which states that for any function \(f(x)\):
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \delta(x-a) \, dx = f(a)
\]
which tells us that the integral of a function multiplied by a Dirac delta function is just the value of the function at the point where the delta function is centered. Applying this property to the integrals in the expression for \(C_{n,m}\) gives:
\[
C_{n,m} = \frac{4 \varepsilon_{n} \varepsilon_{m}}{L_x L_y} \sum_{i=1}^N A_i \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x_i\right) \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y_i\right)
\tag{4.12}\]

title: 1  Analytical solution of the 2D diffusion equation with Neumann boundary conditions
section: 6.1 Confirming the solution for the constant decay rate case
text:
6.1 Confirming the solution for the constant decay rate case
We can confirm this solution by showing that we can arrive at equation Equation 1.1 from equation Equation 6.1 if the following relationship between their corresponding solutions \(u(x,y,t)\) and \(w(x,y,t)\) holds:
\[
w(x,y,t) = u(x,y,t) e^{-\beta t}
\] Let’s find the first time derivative of \(w\) and the Laplacian of \(w\): \[
\frac{\partial w}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} e^{-\beta t} - \beta u e^{-\beta t}
\]
\[
\nabla^2 w =
\left( \frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial y^2} \right) = \left( \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} \right) e^{-\beta t} = \nabla^2 u e^{-\beta t}
\]
Substituting these two expressions into equation Equation 6.1 gives:
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} e^{-\beta t} - \beta u e^{-\beta t} = D \nabla^2 u e^{-\beta t} - \beta u e^{-\beta t}
\]
Then, we can divide both sides by \(e^{-\beta t}\) (which is never zero) to obtain:
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} - \beta u = D \nabla^2 u - \beta u
\]
and then, by adding \(\beta u\) to both sides, we arrive at the original diffusion equation:
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = D \nabla^2 u
\]
This confirms that our proposed solution is correct.
crumbs: 1  Analytical solution of the 2D diffusion equation with Neumann boundary conditions

title: 2  Non-homogeneous case
text:
2.1 Attempting separation of variables
Let’s now consider the non-homogeneous diffusion equation with a constant decay rate \(\beta\) and point-like sources that inject material into the system:
\[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = D \nabla^2 v + Q(x,y,t) - \beta v
\tag{2.1}\]
where \[
Q(x,y,t) = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i(t) \delta(x-x_i) \delta(y-y_i)
\] represents point-like sources located at positions \((x_i,y_i)\) with time-dependent injection rates \(A_i(t) > 0\), and \(v(x,y,t)\) is the new function we want to solve for.
As before, we will assume Neumann boundary conditions on all sides of the rectangular domain of size \(L_x \times L_y\)
If we try to use separation of variables as before, we find that the presence of the non-homogeneous term makes it impossible to separate the variables: \[
\frac{1}{T(t)} \frac{dT}{dt} = D \left( \frac{1}{X(x)} \frac{d^2 X}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{Y(y)} \frac{d^2 Y}{dy^2} \right) + \underbrace{\frac{Q(x,y,t)}{X(x) Y(y) T(t)}}_{
\text{non-separable term}} - \beta
\]
The presence of the non-separable term \(\frac{Q(x,y,t)}{X(x) Y(y) T(t)}\), which depends on all three variables \(x\), \(y\), and \(t\), prevents us from separating the variables.

title: 2  Non-homogeneous case
text:
2.2 Using eigenfunction expansion
We will start by assuming that the solution \(v(x,y,t)\) can be written as a sum of eigenmodes, similar to what we did in the homogeneous case:
\[
v(x,y,t) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} T_{n,m}(t) \phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\tag{2.2}\]
where \(T_{n,m}(t)\) are time-dependent coefficients to be determined and \(\phi_{n,m}(x,y)\) are the eigenfunctions defined as:
\[
\phi_{n,m}(x,y) = \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x} x\right) \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{L_y} y\right)
\]
Similarly, we also need to project the source term \(Q(x,y,t)\) onto the same eigenmodes:
\[
Q(x,y,t)= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} q_{n,m}(t) \phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\]
where \(q_{n,m}(t)\) are the coefficients of the source term expansion. To find these coefficients, we can use the exact same procedure described in Section 4.2 for determining the coefficients using the initial condition, leveraging the orthogonality property of the cosine functions and the sifting property of the delta function.
This leads us to the following expression for \(q_{n,m}(t)\):
\[
q_{n,m}(t) = \frac{4 \varepsilon_n \varepsilon_m}{L_x L_y} \sum_{i=1}^N A_i(t) \phi_{n,m}(x_i,y_i)
\tag{2.3}\]
where
\[
\varepsilon_n = \begin{cases} 1/2 & \text{if } n=0 \\ 1 & \text{if } n>0 \end{cases}
\quad , \quad
\varepsilon_m = \begin{cases} 1/2  & \text{if } m=0 \\ 1 & \text{if } m>0 \end{cases}
\]
Now we can substitute the expansion for \(v(x,y,t)\) and \(Q(x,y,t)\) into the original PDE Equation 4.1. Since the equation is large, we will represent the infinite sum of infinite eigenmodes as \(\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty}\) for brevity:
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left( \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} T_{n,m}(t) \phi_{n,m}(x,y) \right) = D \nabla^2 \left( \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} T_{n,m}(t) \phi_{n,m}(x,y) \right) +
\] \[
\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} q_{n,m}(t) \phi_{n,m}(x,y) - \beta \left( \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} T_{n,m}(t) \phi_{n,m}(x,y) \right)
\] Rearranging the terms gives:
\[
\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} \frac{d T_{n,m}(t)}{dt} \phi_{n,m}(x,y) = D \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} T_{n,m}(t) \nabla^2 \phi_{n,m}(x,y) +
\] \[
\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} q_{n,m}(t) \phi_{n,m}(x,y) - \beta \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} T_{n,m}(t) \phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\]
As shown in Section 4.0.1, we know that the eigenfunctions \(\phi_{n,m}(x,y)\) satisfy the eigenvalue equation:
\[
\nabla^2 \phi_{n,m}(x,y) = -\lambda_{n,m} \phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\]
So we can substitute this into the equation above:
\[
\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} \frac{d T_{n,m}(t)}{dt} \phi_{n,m}(x,y) = -D \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} \lambda_{n,m} T_{n,m}(t) \phi_{n,m}(x,y) +
\] \[
\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} q_{n,m}(t) \phi_{n,m}(x,y) - \beta \sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} T_{n,m}(t) \phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\]
We can now group by the eigenfunctions \(\phi_{n,m}(x,y)\):
\[
\sum_{n,m}^{\infty, \infty} \left( \frac{d T_{n,m}(t)}{dt} + (D \lambda_{n,m} + \beta) T_{n,m}(t) - q_{n,m}(t) \right) \phi_{n,m}(x,y) = 0
\]
This leaves us with an ordinary differential equation for each mode \((n,m)\):
\[
\frac{d T_{n,m}(t)}{dt} + (D \lambda_{n,m} + \beta) T_{n,m}(t) = q_{n,m}(t)
\tag{2.4}\]
This is a first-order linear ODE, which we have to solve for each pair \((n,m)\)
For solving this, we can use the integrating Factor method, where we will use \(e^{k_{n,m} t}\) as the integrating factor, where \(k_{n,m} = D \lambda_{n,m} + \beta\).
Multiplying both sides of equation Equation 2.4 by the integrating factor gives:
\[
e^{k_{n,m} t} \frac{d T_{n,m}(t)}{dt} + k_{n,m} e^{k_{n,m} t} T_{n,m}(t) = q_{n,m}(t) e^{k_{n,m} t}
\]
The left-hand side can be recognized as the derivative of the product \(e^{k_{n,m} t} T_{n,m}(t)\):
\[
\frac{d}{dt} \left( e^{k_{n,m} t} T_{n,m}(t) \right) = q_{n,m}(t) e^{k_{n,m} t}
\]
Integrating both sides with respect to \(t\) from \(0\) to \(t\) gives:
\[
\left[ e^{k_{n,m} t} T_{n,m}(t) \right]_0^t = \int_0^t q_{n,m}(\tau) e^{k_{n,m} \tau} d\tau
\] This simplifies to: \[
e^{k_{n,m} t} T_{n,m}(t) - T_{n,m}(0) = \int_0^t q_{n,m}(\tau) e^{k_{n,m} \tau} d\tau
\]
Solving for \(T_{n,m}(t)\) gives:
\[
T_{n,m}(t) = e^{-k_{n,m} t}  T_{n,m}(0) + \int_0^t q_{n,m}(\tau) e^{-k_{n,m} (t-\tau)} d\tau
\]
We need to determine \(T_{n,m}(0)\) using the initial condition for \(v(x,y,0)\):
\[
v(x,y,0) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} T_{n,m}(0) \phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\]
Using the orthogonality property of the eigenfunctions shown in Section 4.2, we can find \(T_{n,m}(0)\) as:
\[
T_{n,m}(0) = \frac{4 \varepsilon_n \varepsilon_m}{L_x L_y} \int_0^{L_x} \int_0^{L_y} v(x,y,0) \phi_{n,m}(x,y) dy dx
\tag{2.5}\]

title: 2  Non-homogeneous case
text:
2.3 Final solution
Substituting \(T_{n,m}(t)\) back into the eigenfunction expansion for \(v(x,y,t)\) in equation Equation 4.2, we obtain the final solution for the non-homogeneous diffusion equation with point-like sources:
\[
v(x,y,t) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \left[ e^{-k_{n,m} t}  T_{n,m}(0) + \int_0^t q_{n,m}(\tau) e^{-k_{n,m} (t-\tau)} d\tau \right] \phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\] where
\[
k_{n,m} = D \lambda_{n,m} + \beta
\] \[
\lambda_{n,m} = \left( \frac{n \pi}{L_x} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{m \pi}{L_y} \right)^2
\] \[
q_{n,m}(t) = \frac{4 \varepsilon_n \varepsilon_m}{L_x L_y} \sum_{i=1}^N A_i(t) \phi_{n,m}(x_i,y_i)
\] \[
T_{n,m}(0) = \frac{4 \varepsilon_n \varepsilon_m}{L_x L_y} \int_0^{L_x} \int_0^{L_y} v(x,y,0) \phi_{n,m}(x,y) dy dx
\]

title: 2  Non-homogeneous case
text:
2.4 Steady-state solution
Let’s now evaluate the shape of the solution as \(t \to \infty\), which should correspond to the steady-state solution in which \(\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = 0\), assuming that the source terms \(A_i\) are constant in time.
As \(t \to \infty\), the exponential decay term \(e^{-k_{n,m} t}\) approaches zero for all modes \((n,m)\):
\[
\lim_{t \to \infty} e^{-k_{n,m} t} = 0
\]
Thus, the steady-state solution simplifies to:
\[
v_{ss}(x,y) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \left[ q_{n,m} \int_0^{t} e^{-k_{n,m} (t-\tau)} d\tau \right] \phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\] Now let’s solve the integral:
\[
\int_0^{t}  e^{-k_{n,m} (t-\tau)} d\tau \] We can substitute \(u = t - \tau\), which gives \(d\tau = -du\). The limits of integration change accordingly: When \(\tau = 0\), \(u = t\); and when \(\tau = t\), \(u = 0\). Therefore, the integral becomes:
\[
\int_t^{0} e^{-k_{n,m} u} (-du) = \int_0^{t} e^{-k_{n,m} u} du = \left[ -\frac{1}{k_{n,m}} e^{-k_{n,m} u} \right]_0^{t} = \frac{1}{k_{n,m}} \left( 1 - e^{-k_{n,m} t} \right)
\]
Taking the limit as \(t \to \infty\), we find:
\[
\lim_{t \to \infty} \int_0^{t}  e^{-k_{n,m} (t-\tau)} d\tau = \frac{1}{k_{n,m}}
\]
Thus, the steady-state solution becomes:
\[
v_{ss}(x,y) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{q_{n,m}}{k_{n,m}} \phi_{n,m}(x,y)
\] where \[
k_{n,m} = D \lambda_{n,m} + \beta
\] \[
\lambda_{n,m} = \left( \frac{n \pi}{L_x} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{m \pi}{L_y} \right)^2
\] \[
q_{n,m} = \frac{4 \varepsilon_n \varepsilon_m}{L_x L_y} \sum_{i=1}^N A_i \phi_{n,m}(x_i,y_i)
\]
We can confirm that this is the steady-state solution if we derive the solution directly from the steady-state version of the original PDE Equation 4.1, which is:
\[
0 = D \nabla^2 v_{ss} + Q(x,y) - \beta v_{ss}
\] Rearranging gives:
\[
D \nabla^2 v_{ss} - \beta v_{ss} = - Q(x,y)
\]
This is known as the inhomogeneous Helmholtz equation (also called the screened Poisson equation).

title: 2  Non-homogeneous case
3  Effective solution
4  Mixed boundary conditions
text:
4.1 Finding eigenfunctions with mixed boundary conditions
Let’s consider the same non-homogeneous diffusion equation described in Chapter 2
\[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = D \nabla^2 v + Q(x,y,t) - \beta v
\tag{4.1}\]
where \[
Q(x,y,t) = \sum_{i=1}^N A_i \delta(x-x_i) \delta(y-y_i)
\] represents point-like sources located at positions \((x_i,y_i)\), with production rates \(A_i\). This time, we will impose mixed boundary conditions on one edge of the domain. This is with the goal of modeling the microfluidic device as a rectangular domain which has 3 impermeable walls (Neumann boundary conditions) and one edge that connects the chamber to an external reservoir, allowing for diffusion across the domain (Robin boundary condition).
For reflective (Neumann) boundaries: \[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=0} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=L_x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\Big|_{y=0} = 0
\] For the Robin boundary at \(y=L_y\):
\[
-D \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\Big|_{y=L_y} =J= k (v(x,L_y,t) - v_{ext})
\]
\(J\) is the diffusion flux across the Robin boundary in the outward normal direction, and it is proportional to the concentration difference between the interior part of the domain at \(y=L_y\) and an external reservoir with concentration \(v_{ext}\), \(D\) is the diffusion coefficient, \(k\) is the mass transfer coefficient. For simplicity, we will assume that \(v_{ext}\) is zero.
Let’s solve this equation using 2 different methods: Eigenfunction expansion and Green’s functions.
But first, we need to find the eigenfunctions that satisfy the mixed boundary conditions.
To find the eigenfunctions, we start with the spatial eigenvalue problem associated with the homogeneous part of the diffusion equation:
\[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = D \nabla^2 v - \beta v
\tag{4.2}\] We assume that the solution can be separated into spatial and temporal parts:
\[
v(x,y,t) = X(x) Y(y) T(t)
\]
Substituting this into Equation 4.2 gives:
\[
XY \frac{dT}{dt} = D T \left( Y \frac{d^2X}{dx^2} + X \frac{d^2Y}{dy^2} \right) - \beta XYT
\] Dividing both sides by \(XYTD\) leads to:
\[
\frac{1}{D T} \frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{1}{X} \frac{d^2X}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{Y} \frac{d^2Y}{dy^2} - \frac{\beta}{D}
\] reorganizing terms, we have: \[
\frac{1}{D T} \frac{dT}{dt} + \frac{\beta}{D} = \frac{1}{X} \frac{d^2X}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{Y} \frac{d^2Y}{dy^2}
\]
since the left side depends only on time and the right side only on space, both sides must equal a constant, which we denote as \(-\lambda\). This gives us two separate equations:
\[
\frac{1}{D T} \frac{dT}{dt} + \frac{\beta}{D} = -\lambda
\] \[
\frac{1}{X} \frac{d^2X}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{Y} \frac{d^2Y}{dy^2} = -\lambda
\] This gives us 3 ordinary differential equations:
\[\frac{dT}{dt} = -(\lambda + \frac{\beta}{D}) DT \tag{4.3}\] \[\frac{d^2X}{dx^2} = -\lambda_x X \tag{4.4}\] \[\frac{d^2Y}{dy^2} = -\lambda_y Y \tag{4.5}\] with the constraint that \(\lambda = \lambda_x + \lambda_y\).
The solution to Equation 4.3 is:
\[
T(t) = T(0) e^{-(\lambda + \frac{\beta}{D}) Dt}
\]
Next, we need to solve Equation 4.4 and Equation 4.5. As shown in Section 3.1, the general solutions are:
\[
X(x) = A_x \cos(\sqrt{\lambda_x} x) + B_x \sin(\sqrt{\lambda_x} x)
\] \[
Y(y) = A_y \cos(\sqrt{\lambda_y} y) + B_y \sin(\sqrt{\lambda_y} y)
\]
Let’s apply the boundary conditions to find the constants and the allowed values of \(\lambda_x\) and \(\lambda_y\).
For the Neumann boundary conditions at \(x=0\) and \(x=L_x\): \[
\frac{dXYT}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} = YT \frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} = 0
\] \(Y\) and \(T\) can not be zero for all \(y\) and \(t\), so we have: \[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=0} = 0 \implies B_x = 0
\] Next, we apply the Neumann boundary condition at \(x=L_x\): \[
\frac{dX}{dx}\Big|_{x=L_x} = 0 \implies -A_x \sqrt{\lambda_x} \sin(\sqrt{\lambda_x} L_x) = 0
\] This leads to the allowed values of \(\lambda_x\): \[\sqrt{\lambda_x} L_x = n \pi \implies \lambda_x = \left(\frac{n \pi}{L_x}\right)^2, \quad n \in \mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}\]
Thus, the eigenfunctions in the \(x\) direction are: \[\boxed{
X_n(x) = A_n \cos\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L_x}\right)}\]
Now, let’s apply the reflective boundary condition at \(y=0\): \[
\frac{dY}{dy}\Big|_{y=0} = 0 \implies B_y = 0
\]
Next, we apply the Robin boundary condition at \(y=L_y\):
\[
-D \frac{d YXT}{dy}\Big|_{y=L_y} = k (Y(L_y)XT - v_{ext})
\]
We will assume \(v_{ext}=0\). Dividing both sides by \(XT\), we get:
\[
-D \frac{dY}{dy}\Big|_{y=L_y} = k (Y(L_y))
\] Substituting the expression for \(Y(y)\), we have: \[
-D \left(-A_y \sqrt{\lambda_y} \sin(\sqrt{\lambda_y} L_y)\right) = k \left(A_y \cos(\sqrt{\lambda_y} L_y)\right)
\] Rearranging terms, we obtain the following equation: \[ \tan(\sqrt{\lambda_y} L_y) = \frac{k}{D \sqrt{\lambda_y}} \]
Let’s plot the left and right sides of this equation to find the allowed values of \(\lambda_y\).
Code
Plotly = require("plotly.js-dist@2")

k = 10
D = 1
Ly = 1

x = Array.from({length: 2000}, (_, i) => (i + 1) * 0.005) // avoid xi=0

// Tune these:
YMAX = 10          // don’t draw tan outside [-YMAX, YMAX]
COS_EPS = 1e-3     // don’t draw near asymptotes where cos≈0
pointsX = [1.43, 4.315, 7.25]
pointsY = pointsX.map(xi => k / (D * xi))
y1 = x.map(xi => {
  const u = xi * Ly
  const c = Math.cos(u)
  if (Math.abs(c) < COS_EPS) return null     // break line near asymptotes
  const t = Math.tan(u)
  if (!Number.isFinite(t)) return null
  if (Math.abs(t) > YMAX) return null        // optional: also clip large values
  return t
})

y2 = x.map(xi => k / (D * xi)) // this has a singularity at 0; x starts > 0

plot = {
  const div = document.createElement("div")
  div.style.height = "400px"
  div.style.width = "600px"

  Plotly.newPlot(div, [
    {x, y: y1, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "tan(√λy * Ly)"},
    {x, y: y2, type: "scatter", mode: "lines", name: "k / (D * √λy)"},
    {
      x: pointsX,
      y: pointsY,
      type: "scatter",
      mode: "markers",
      name: "solutions",
      marker: {color: "red", size: 8}
    }
  ], {
    title: "Finding Eigenvalues λy",
    xaxis: {title: "√λy"},
    yaxis: {title: "Value", range: [-1, 10]},
    width: 600,
    height: 400,
    margin: {l: 20, r: 0, b: 30, t: 30}
  })

  return div
}
